Every connection in the book starts with a long `ssh` command: a key file, a user, an IP address, and sometimes a couple of `-o` options. SSH can read all of these from a file at `~/.ssh/config`, so the command shrinks to `ssh <alias>`. This appendix pulls together the SSH settings from [AWS Server Login](aws-ssh-ec2.qmd), [Managing SSH Key Pairs](manage-ssh-keys.qmd), and [Linux Commands](linux-commands.qmd) in one place.

## Creating the file

The config file lives on our local machine (not the EC2 instance). Create it if it doesn't exist, then restrict it to our own account:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
touch ~/.ssh/config
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/config
```

SSH applies the same permission rules here as it does to keys (see [SSH directory and file permissions](aws-ssh-ec2.qmd#ssh-directory-and-file-permissions)). If `~/.ssh/config` is writable by other users, SSH refuses to read it and prints `Bad owner or permissions on ~/.ssh/config`.

## A basic entry

Each entry starts with a `Host` line followed by indented settings:

```{verbatim}
Host aws-dev
    HostName YOUR_PUBLIC_IP_ADDRESS
    User ec2-user
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/aws-dev.pem
```

| Setting        | Replaces                  | Meaning                                         |
| -------------- | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `Host`         | (nothing)                 | The alias we type after `ssh`                   |
| `HostName`     | `@YOUR_PUBLIC_IP_ADDRESS` | The public IP or Public DNS name of the instance |
| `User`         | `ec2-user@`               | The login user for the AMI                      |
| `IdentityFile` | `-i ~/.ssh/aws-dev.pem`   | The private key to present                      |

With the entry saved, these two commands do the same thing:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
ssh -i ~/.ssh/aws-dev.pem ec2-user@YOUR_PUBLIC_IP_ADDRESS
ssh aws-dev
```

The alias also works with `scp`, so copying files from [Upgrade to Amazon Linux 2023](upgrade-al2023.qmd) becomes `scp aws-dev:~/.bashrc ./bashrc-al2`.

## Forcing a single key

`IdentityFile` (like `-i`) only suggests a key. SSH still offers every key held by `ssh-agent`, and it offers them first. Two things can go wrong:

1. If the agent holds a key the server also accepts, that key wins and the key file is never tested.

2. If the agent holds several keys the server doesn't accept, the server stops listening after its limit (six attempts by default) and closes the connection with `Too many authentication failures` before our key gets a turn.

On the command line we fixed this with two options (see [Linux Commands](linux-commands.qmd)):

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
ssh -i ~/.ssh/aws-dev.pem -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -o IdentityAgent=none ec2-user@YOUR_PUBLIC_IP_ADDRESS
```

In the config file, the same options become two more lines in the entry (written without the `=`):

```{verbatim}
Host aws-dev
    HostName YOUR_PUBLIC_IP_ADDRESS
    User ec2-user
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/aws-dev.pem
    IdentitiesOnly yes
    IdentityAgent none
```

* `IdentitiesOnly yes` restricts SSH to the key named in `IdentityFile`.

* `IdentityAgent none` turns off `ssh-agent` for this host, so no agent keys are offered.

## Several entries

One file can hold an entry for each user and key we use. With the keys from [Managing SSH Key Pairs](manage-ssh-keys.qmd) and the `test-user` account from [Linux Users](linux-users.qmd), the file on the System76 machine might look like this:

```{verbatim}
# Recovery access with the AWS key pair
Host aws-dev
    HostName YOUR_PUBLIC_IP_ADDRESS
    User ec2-user
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/aws-dev.pem
    IdentitiesOnly yes
    IdentityAgent none

# Routine access with our own key
Host my-ec2
    HostName YOUR_PUBLIC_IP_ADDRESS
    User ec2-user
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/<your-key-name>
    IdentitiesOnly yes

# Non-root user
Host my-ec2-test
    HostName YOUR_PUBLIC_IP_ADDRESS
    User test-user
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/<your-key-name>
    IdentitiesOnly yes
```

On the MacBook, the same aliases point to the machine specific key (`IdentityFile ~/.ssh/<your-key-name>-macbook`). Private keys never leave the machine that made them; only the config entries look alike.

The routine entries keep the agent on (no `IdentityAgent none`), which is useful when the key has a passphrase that the agent remembers. `IdentitiesOnly yes` still stops the agent from offering its other keys.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="First match wins"}

SSH reads the file from top to bottom and keeps the first value it finds for each setting. A catch all `Host *` block for shared defaults belongs at the end of the file; placed at the top, it overrides every entry below it.

:::

## When the IP changes

A stopped instance gets a new public IP when it starts (unless it has an Elastic IP), so `HostName` goes stale. Look up the new address from the local machine:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
aws ec2 describe-instances \
  --instance-ids YOUR_INSTANCE_ID \
  --query "Reservations[*].Instances[*].PublicIpAddress" \
  --output text \
  --profile dev-deploy
```

Then edit the `HostName` line of each entry for that instance. That's the only change; the aliases, users, and keys stay the same. The Public DNS name from [Using the Public DNS](aws-ssh-ec2.qmd#using-the-public-dns) works as a `HostName` too, but it encodes the IP, so it changes at the same time.

Two other things go stale with a new IP:

* SSH asks to confirm the host key again, because `~/.ssh/known_hosts` stores keys by address (see [Host key verification](aws-ssh-ec2.qmd#host-key-verification)).

* If our own home IP changed, the port 22 rule in the security group no longer matches and `ssh` ends with `Connection timed out`. That's a security group problem, not a config problem (see [Security Group doesn't allow SSH (port 22)](aws-ssh-ec2.qmd#security-group-doesnt-allow-ssh-port-22)).

## Checking the config

`ssh -G` prints the settings SSH would use for an alias without connecting:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
ssh -G aws-dev | grep -E '^(hostname|user|port|identityfile|identitiesonly|identityagent) '
```

::: {style="font-style: italic;"}

```{verbatim}
user ec2-user
hostname YOUR_PUBLIC_IP_ADDRESS
port 22
identitiesonly yes
identityagent none
identityfile ~/.ssh/aws-dev.pem
```

:::

If a value is missing or wrong, the entry has a typo or an earlier block already set it. To watch the settings in use during a real connection, add `-v` (`ssh -v aws-dev`); the debug lines show the config file being read and each key SSH offers.

## Recap

1. `~/.ssh/config` lives on the local machine, needs `600` permissions, and turns a long `ssh` command into `ssh <alias>`.

2. `IdentitiesOnly yes` and `IdentityAgent none` make SSH use only the key in `IdentityFile`, which prevents `Too many authentication failures`.

3. One entry per user and key keeps recovery (`.pem`) and routine access separate.

4. When the instance gets a new IP, update `HostName`; nothing else in the entry changes.
